questions.text: Hippopotamus loves to wallow in ____ mud.
questions.explanation: “Mud” is an uncountable noun used generally here, so it takes no article.

questions.text: The Principal welcomed the students ____ the school.
questions.explanation: The verb “welcome” takes “to” when naming the destination: welcome someone to the school.

questions.text: I love having ____ eggs for breakfast.
questions.explanation: The plural noun “eggs” is used generically, so no article is needed.

questions.text: I have ____ of things on my mind.
questions.explanation: “A lot of” is the natural quantifier before the plural count noun “things”.

questions.text: The members of the choir ____ every Saturday.
questions.explanation: “Members” is plural, so the present-simple verb is “meet”.

questions.text: The Aryans are ____ European stock.
questions.explanation: The standard expression is “of European stock,” indicating ancestry or origin.

questions.text: John was ____ at the surprising turn of events.
questions.explanation: Both “surprised” and “amazed” are grammatically possible with “at”; no unique answer can be justified from the item as transcribed.

questions.text: Such a gruesome event ____ never happened in the locality before.
questions.explanation: “An event has never happened” uses the present perfect to describe experience up to now.

questions.text: Cleopatra was said to be an ____ beauty in her time.
questions.explanation: All four options are near-synonyms and can grammatically complete the sentence; context does not uniquely select one.

questions.text: The delegates ____ since morning to meet the CEO.
questions.explanation: The natural construction is “have been waiting since morning”; that option is absent, so no listed option is fully correct.

questions.text: The divers dived deep ____ the sea to locate the ship.
questions.explanation: “Into the sea” expresses movement from the surface to a position inside the sea.

questions.text: By the time the concert ended, the children ____ already asleep.
questions.explanation: The past perfect “had been” places the children’s state of being asleep before the concert ended.

questions.text: Despite ____, the Judge was moved to pity.
questions.explanation: “Despite his hard-heartedness” contrasts his lack of sympathy with the judge’s eventual pity.

questions.text: The girls cheered ____ when their team scored a goal.
questions.explanation: Both “loudly” and “wildly” can naturally describe cheering; the sentence does not establish a unique choice.

questions.text: You've understood, ____?
questions.explanation: The positive statement “You have understood” takes the negative question tag “haven’t you?”

questions.text: Neither of the candidates ____ for the debate.
questions.explanation: “Showed up” is plausible in past narration, while “shows up” can be generic; the isolated sentence gives insufficient time context.

questions.text: ____ and lodging are available here.
questions.explanation: The established expression is “food and lodging.”

questions.text: Walking ____ the best way to stay fit.
questions.explanation: A gerund phrase used as the subject takes a singular verb: “Walking is…”

questions.text: Because of global warming, the climate ____ changed a lot.
questions.explanation: “Has changed” is present perfect, describing a change from the past with relevance to the present.

questions.text: Democracy without freedom is ____.
questions.explanation: Without freedom, democracy loses its essential meaning; “meaningless” completes the sentence.

questions.text: He was so passionate about the job, he was like ____.
questions.explanation: “A man on a mission” describes someone strongly driven by a purpose, matching the context of passion.

questions.text: Who ____ to apply for the post of Treasurer?
questions.explanation: “Who” is the subject of the singular verb “wants” in this question.

questions.text: We can eat in the café ____ order a takeout.
questions.explanation: “Or” connects the two alternatives: eating at the café or ordering takeout.

questions.text: She succeeded ____ everyone failed.
questions.explanation: “Where” introduces the contrasting circumstance/place in which she succeeded while others failed.

questions.text: Choose the word that best completes the source sentence: ____.
questions.explanation: The source sentence/prompt is missing or illegible in the transcription; answer cannot be determined safely.

questions.text: She could not convince the jury ____ her pleas.
Please don't walk ____ the grass.
questions.explanation: The standard collocation is “walk on the grass.”

questions.text: Good heavens! How time ____.
questions.explanation: “How time flies!” is the fixed exclamation expressing how quickly time passes.

questions.text: Her job comes with a ____ pay package.
questions.explanation: “Hefty” means large or substantial, commonly used to describe a generous pay package.

questions.text: Jim was already in bed when I ____ him last night.
questions.explanation: “Last night” sets a past time; the completed action is expressed by “called.”

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) The bulldozer made a humming noise. (ii) The noise irritated people nearby. (iii) They complained against the irritated bulldozer.
questions.explanation: Statements (i) and (ii) are grammatically sound. Statement (iii) wrongly describes the bulldozer as irritated; it should refer to the people.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) The guests were treated to a lavish meal. (ii) They ate until they were full. (iii) That dinner party was talked about for a long time.
questions.explanation: All three sentences are grammatically correct and form a coherent sequence about the dinner party.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) Ram was known for his eloquence. (ii) Ram was invited to speech on the meeting. (iii) At the last minute, he had to cancel the program.
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (iii) are correct. “Invited to speech on the meeting” in (ii) is not grammatical; it would be “invited to speak at the meeting.”

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) The aeroplane glided smooth in the blue sky. (ii) The passengers leaned back in their seats. (iii) It was such a comfortable flight.
questions.explanation: Sentences (ii) and (iii) are correct. In (i), the adverb “smoothly” is required instead of the adjective “smooth.”

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) John is such a good swimmer. (ii) He could swam in any sea. (iii) He once swam in the English Channel.
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (iii) are correct. After the modal “could,” the base form “swim,” not “swam,” is required in (ii).

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) Isn't he the Principal of the school? (ii) I heard that he's a man of integrity. (iii) He combines strictness with approachability.
questions.explanation: All three sentences are grammatical: the question, the report of his integrity, and the statement about his balanced leadership.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) Can you do me favor? (ii) Can you favor me? (iii) Can you do me this favor please?
questions.explanation: Sentences (ii) and (iii) are acceptable. Sentence (i) is missing the article in “do me a favor.”

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) He told us a very interesting story. (ii) The interesting listeners were captivated. (iii) Nobody wanted the story to end.
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (iii) are correct. In (ii), “interesting listeners” should be “interested listeners.”

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) How many books do you wish to buy? (ii) How many books did she wish to buy? (iii) You wish to buy books how many?
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (ii) use correct question word order. Sentence (iii) places “how many” incorrectly.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) Jim was the monitor in class for five years. (ii) Jim was the class monitor for five years. (iii) Jim had been a class monitor for five years.
questions.explanation: The distinction between “monitor in class” and “class monitor” is not decisive enough to exclude (i); the intended grammar criterion is unclear.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) I've never seen a tiger at close range. (ii) I've never seen a tiger this close. (iii) I've never seen a tiger close up.
questions.explanation: All three expressions—“at close range,” “this close,” and “close up”—are acceptable ways to describe seeing a tiger nearby.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) She's a famous actress of yesteryears. (ii) She's a famous actress yesterday. (iii) She was once a famous actress.
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (iii) are correct. “She's a famous actress yesterday” in (ii) is ungrammatical.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) After the harvest, the farmer went to bed happy. (ii) The good harvest made the farmer happy. (iii) After the harvest, the farmer went happy to bed.
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (ii) are natural and grammatical. “Went happy to bed” in (iii) is not the usual grammatical placement.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) The current is too strong to cross. (ii) The current is too wide to cross. (iii) The current is too powerful to cross.
questions.explanation: “Too wide to cross” can describe the width of a water current/channel in context, so the item does not securely distinguish the intended pair.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) The Sun is too heat today. (ii) The Sun is too hot today. (iii) The Sun is so hot today.
questions.explanation: Sentences (ii) and (iii) are correct. “Too heat” in (i) incorrectly uses the noun “heat” where the adjective “hot” is needed.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) Don't you have anything better to do? (ii) Don't you have anything to do with your time? (iii) Don't you have anything useful to do?
questions.explanation: All three sentences can be acceptable in context; sentence (ii) is less idiomatic but not clearly ungrammatical.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) For heaven's sake, stop wasting your time! (ii) For heaven's sake, stop waste time! (iii) For heaven's sake, stop wasting time!
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (iii) are correct. After “stop,” the gerund “wasting” is required in this construction.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) She's a strong, confident woman. (ii) She exudes confident. (iii) Her confidence is admired by many.
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (iii) are correct. “Exudes confident” is incorrect because the noun “confidence” is required.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) Which pairs of shoes do you prefer? (ii) Which pair of shoes do you prefer? (iii) Which of these pairs do you prefer?
questions.explanation: Each construction can be grammatical depending on whether the speaker is asking about multiple pairs, one pair, or a set of pairs; context is missing.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentences: (i) The restaurant opens at all hours. (ii) The restaurant opens 24x7. (iii) The restaurant is opening at all times.
questions.explanation: Sentences (i) and (ii) express regular or continuous opening hours correctly. “Is opening at all times” is not idiomatic for a regular schedule.
